length(new_age)

#Question 2

rep(c("A","B"), each = 2)
rep(c("A","B"), times = 2)
#each repeats every element individually before moving to the next one. So “A” is repeated 2 times, then “B” is repeated 2 times.
#times repeats the whole vector from start to finish. So the full sequence “A”, “B” is copied 2 times.

#Question 3

seq(1, 20, by = 2)
seq(1, 20, length.out = 5)

#by controls the step size.
#length.out controls the number of elements you want.
#Use by when the interval itself matters and is fixed. Use length.out when you need a set number of points that cover a range exactly, for example 100 evenly spaced x-values to plot a smooth curve, or 5 evenly spaced cutoffs between the minimum and maximum of a variable.

grades[3]

#Question 5
#Negative indexing is useful when you know exactly which position to drop, such as removing the first row of a data vector that holds a header or a label by mistake. Logical indexing is the better tool when you don’t know the positions in advance and want to filter by a condition, such as picking out all students whose grades are at least 85 to give them honors recognition, using grades[grades >= 85].

#Question 6
#The grades vector only has 5 elements, so position 10 does not exist. R returns NA, which stands for a missing value. The name also shows as <NA> because there is no name attached to a position that doesn’t exist.

#Question 8
#When the two vectors were added together, R noticed that short was too small to match z element-by-element, so it automatically repeated short from the beginning until it reached the same length as z. Since z has 6 elements and short has 2, R cycled through short three times, turning it into c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0) behind the scenes, and then performed the addition normally.

#Question 9
z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
print(z + c(1, 0, 1))
print(z + c(1, 0, 1, 1))
#Adding z to c(1, 0, 1) works cleanly with no warning because 6 is an exact multiple of 3, so R can recycle the shorter vector a whole number of times without any leftover elements. Adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) however triggers a warning because 6 is not an exact multiple of 4

```{r}
#Part D

student <- list(
  name       = "Maria Santos",
  age        = 20,
  grades     = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)
print(student)

print(student["grades"])
print(class(student["grades"]))

print(student[["grades"]])
print(class(student[["grades"]]))
print(student$name)
print(student[["grades"]][2])
```

#Question 10
#Running class(student["grades"]) returns "list", while class(student[["grades"]]) returns "numeric". Single brackets [ ] treat the list like a container and return a smaller list that still wraps the element inside it. Double brackets [[ ]] is a level deeper and pull out the element itself.

#Question 11
#A vector can only hold elements of a single data type: all numbers, or all strings, but never both at once. A list, can hold anything: a number, a string, another list, a data frame, a function — all mixed together.

```{r}
#Part E

inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
print(inventory$item[inventory$in_stock == TRUE])

inventory$item     <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price    <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
print(inventory)
```
